**Battleship Potemkin and the Odessa Steps**
Sergei Eisenstein's 1925 Soviet silent film about the 1905 mutiny aboard the Potemkin, which begins when sailors are served maggot-infested meat. Its "Odessa Steps" sequence, a showcase of Eisenstein's montage theory, includes a woman shot through her glasses, a baby carriage rolling down the steps, and three shots of stone lions edited to seem to rise. Lev Kuleshov, another Soviet pioneer, showed the power of editing by intercutting one shot of an actor's face with a bowl of soup and a girl in a coffin.

**Black Square and Suprematism**
Kazimir Malevich founded Suprematism, an abstract movement of pure geometric forms that he described as "the supremacy of pure emotion" in his manifesto The Non-Objective World. His Black Square grew out of his designs for the 1913 Futurist opera Victory Over the Sun and was hung high in a corner, where an icon would traditionally go, at the 1915 "0,10" exhibition in Petrograd.

**White on White**
Malevich's 1918 Suprematist painting of a tilted white square on a slightly different white background, which nearly eliminates color altogether.

**Barge Haulers on the Volga**
Ilya Repin's realist painting of eleven exhausted burlaki (barge haulers), including a young boy, harnessed with leather straps and dragging a boat along the banks of the Volga, Russia's longest river.

**Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge**
El Lissitzky's 1919 Civil War propaganda poster, in which a red triangle pierces a white circle, symbolizing the Bolshevik Reds defeating the anti-Communist Whites. Lissitzky also created the abstract Proun series and the photomontage self-portrait The Constructor, and the poster influenced Constructivism, the movement associated with Vladimir Tatlin's unbuilt Tatlin's Tower.

**Wassily Kandinsky and The Blue Rider**
Moscow-born pioneer of abstract art whose painting The Blue Rider, showing a cloaked rider on a white horse, named the Der Blaue Reiter group he co-founded with Franz Marc in Munich. In Concerning the Spiritual in Art, he divided his works into "Impressions," "Improvisations," and "Compositions"; he later taught at the Bauhaus, where he made the Small Worlds prints.

**"Muddle Instead of Music"**
The 1936 Pravda editorial attacking Dmitri Shostakovich's opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, in which Katerina poisons her father-in-law's mushrooms with rat poison and finally drowns along with a rival in a freezing river. Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony was later described as "a Soviet artist's response to just criticism."

**Leningrad Symphony and the "invasion theme"**
Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony commemorates the Nazi siege of Leningrad and features a long, repeating "invasion theme" built up in a huge crescendo. Bartók parodied this theme in the "Interrupted Intermezzo" of his Concerto for Orchestra.

**Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan**
Repin's painting of the tsar clutching his dying son's bloodied head in horror after striking him in a rage. Other Repin clues include They Did Not Expect Him (a political exile's surprise return home), Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks (laughing Cossacks writing an insulting letter to Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV), and Sadko, showing a legendary bard in an underwater kingdom.

**Rayonism and Natalia Goncharova**
An abstract movement founded by Mikhail Larionov and Natalia Goncharova that depicted rays of light reflecting off objects, first shown at the 1913 Target exhibition. Goncharova, who drew on Russian folk art and was part of the Donkey's Tail group, painted The Cyclist, and her Picking Apples set an auction record for a female artist.

**The Wanderers (Peredvizhniki)**
A cooperative of realist painters named for their traveling exhibitions, which brought art to provincial Russian towns from 1871 onward. Members included Repin, as well as Ivan Shishkin and Konstantin Savitsky, who painted Morning in a Pine Forest together.

**Fabergé eggs**
Jeweled Easter eggs made by the House of Peter Carl Fabergé for the Romanov imperial family, about 50 in all. The 1897 Coronation Egg, in yellow enamel and gold modeled on a coronation robe, contains a miniature replica of the coronation carriage as its surprise.

**The Apotheosis of War**
Vasily Vereshchagin's painting of a pyramid of skulls in a desert, dedicated "to all great conquerors, past, present and to come."

**Man with a Movie Camera**
Dziga Vertov's 1929 Soviet documentary demonstrating his "Kino-Eye" theory that the camera can see more than the human eye, including a cameraman setting up on top of a giant camera. Vertov also made Kino-Pravda ("film-truth"), a series of 23 newsreels.

**The Nutcracker's "Russian Dance"**
Tchaikovsky's ballet The Nutcracker includes a divertissement of national dances (Spanish chocolate, Arabian coffee, Chinese tea) along with the "Russian Dance," a lively trepak. Tchaikovsky also wrote Sleeping Beauty, with its "Rose Adagio," and Stravinsky's Petrushka is set at a Shrovetide Fair in St. Petersburg.
